For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

### Short answer **Yes – you can keep the registry, but present it in a way that feels optional and considerate.** --- ## Why a registry is actually helpful (and not rude) | Reason | How it helps your guests | How it helps you | |--------|--------------------------|-----------------| | **Clarity** | No guess‑work about size, color, or style. | You receive items you truly need or want. | | **Budget‑friendly** | Guests can pick something that fits their budget (most registries show price ranges). | You avoid duplicate or unwanted gifts. | | **Convenience** | One‑click ordering, shipping to your address, and often free returns. | Less post‑wedding “thank‑you” hassle. | | **Inclusivity** | Many registries let guests contribute to a honeymoon fund, charity, or “experience” gifts if they prefer not to buy a physical item. | You get experiences or cash that can be used where you need it most. | Most modern registries are **opt‑in tools**, not mandates. The key is how you (and your mother) frame the information. --- ## How to present the registry so it feels polite and optional 1. **Use a “soft” wording on the invitation or wedding website** *Example:* > “Your presence is the greatest gift we could ask for. If you’d like to help us start our new life together, we’ve created a small registry for ideas.” 2. **Separate the registry link from the main invitation** - Put the link on a wedding website, a separate “registry” card, or a QR code on a table‑top sign at the reception. - Guests who don’t want to use it can simply ignore it. 3. **Offer a variety of options** - **Traditional items** (kitchenware, linens, etc.) - **Cash or honeymoon fund** (via platforms like Honeyfund, Zola, or a personal PayPal link) - **Charitable donations** (if you have a cause you care about) - **Experience gifts** (cooking class, spa day, adventure outing) Giving multiple categories lets guests choose what feels most comfortable. 4. **Include a “no‑pressure” note** - A brief line on the registry page: > “Your love and company are more than enough. The registry is simply a suggestion for those who wish to give a gift.” 5. **Make the registry easy to navigate** - Use a platform that groups items by price range (e.g., “Under $50,” “$50‑$100,” “$100+”). - Highlight a few “must‑haves” and a few “nice‑to‑have” items so guests can see the spectrum. 6. **Thank‑you etiquette** - Send personalized thank‑you notes promptly. - Mention the specific gift and why it matters to you; this reinforces that the registry helped you receive exactly what you needed. --- ## Addressing Mom’s Concern Directly 1. **Acknowledge her feeling** > “I understand why it might feel like we’re telling people what to buy, Mom. We really appreciate that you want us to be gracious hosts.” 2. **Explain the purpose** > “The registry isn’t a demand; it’s just a guide for guests who want a little help picking something that fits our home and lifestyle.” 3. **Offer a compromise** - **Create a “suggested gifts” list** (a short, informal list of a few items) **instead of a full‑blown registry**. - **Add a “donate to our honeymoon” option** for guests who prefer cash. - **Include a charitable donation option** if you think that would resonate with your family’s values. 4. **Invite her input** - Ask Mom to review the list and suggest any changes. When she feels part of the process, the registry feels less like a directive and more like a family collaboration. --- ## Quick “Do‑or‑Don’t” Checklist | ✅ Do | ❌ Don’t | |------|----------| | Phrase the registry as *optional* and *suggestive*. | Put the registry link on the main invitation without any context. | | Offer a range of price points and non‑material options. | Assume every guest will buy something from the list. | | Keep the link on a separate page/QR code. | Make the registry the only way to give a gift. | | Thank guests personally for whatever they give. | Send generic thank‑you notes that feel impersonal. | --- ## Sample wording you could use (feel free to tweak) > **Our Wedding Registry** > We feel incredibly lucky to have you celebrate with us. If you’d like to give a gift, we’ve put together a few ideas that would help us start our life together. No pressure at all—your presence is the best present! > 👉 [Link to registry] (or QR code) > **Other ways to celebrate** > • Contribute to our honeymoon fund > • Donate to [Charity Name] in our honor > • Give a handwritten note, recipe, or favorite song—anything that makes us smile! --- ### Bottom line A registry is a **tool**, not a demand. By framing it as a *helpful suggestion* and giving guests multiple ways to contribute (or not), you respect both your guests’ preferences and your mother’s sensibility. Keep the tone light, optional, and inclusive, and you’ll have a registry that feels polite, useful, and—most importantly—welcome to everyone involved. Congratulations, and happy planning
